quote: Suche zu beweisen, dass wenn $f(x)$ eine ganze ganzzahlige irreducible Function und $p$ eine beliebige Primzahl ist, es immer eine Potenz von $p$ giebt, derart, dass $f(x)$ nach dieser Potenz im Sinne der Congruenz irreducibel ist;
english: Try to prove that if $f(x)$ is an irreducible integral polynomial with integer coefficients and $p$ is an arbitrary prime, there always exists a power of $p$ such that $f(x)$ is irreducible modulo this power in the sense of congruence.
topic: Notes on deriving a theorem from the theorem on perspective triangles without continuity axioms, an analogue of Hoppe's theorem on tetrahedra with equal-area faces in four or more dimensions, and a conjecture on irreducibility of integral polynomials modulo prime powers.

triage.modern_statement: Let f ∈ Z[x] be irreducible over Q (or Z), and let p be any prime. Hilbert asks whether there is always some k ≥ 1 such that f cannot be written as g·h (mod p^k) with g and h non-constant integer polynomials. In other words, is every irreducible integer polynomial irreducible modulo some power of every prime?
triage.answered_by: As stated, the claim is false, and Hensel's lemma (Kurt Hensel, starting with his 1897 introduction of p-adic numbers) shows why. Suppose f mod p factors into coprime non-constant factors. Then Hensel lifting carries that factorization to every modulus p^k, and to Z_p. A simple counterexample: x^2+1 is irreducible over Z, but x^2+1 ≡ (x-2)(x+2) mod 5, with coprime factors. So it lifts to a factorization mod 5^k for every k. Similarly, x^4+1 is irreducible over Z but reducible mod every prime. For odd p the reduction is squarefree, so its factorization lifts to all powers of p. My searches found no source that discusses Hilbert's note itself; the refutation is my own inference from the standard Hensel lifting theorem.

evidence.claim: Hensel's lemma: a factorization modulo p (with coprime factors) lifts to factorizations modulo every power of p, and to a factorization over the p-adic integers.
Hensel first explicitly introduced the p-adic numbers in his 1897 paper 'Über eine neue Begründung der Theorie der algebraischen Zahlen'.
x^4+1 is irreducible in Z[x] but reducible modulo every prime.

At the end of the 19th century, Hilbert himself gave examples of irreducible polynomials in Z[x] that are reducible modulo all primes (the family x^4+2ax^2+b^2). Combined with Hensel lifting, these show the conjecture fails.
Factorization modulo p^k and lifting of factorizations (Hensel's lemma, Hen18) are still studied algorithmically today.

triage.why: The conjecture is not one of Hilbert's published problems. It is disproved by an elementary consequence of Hensel's lemma. Any irreducible f whose reduction mod p splits into coprime non-constant factors stays reducible mod p^k for all k, for example x^2+1 with p=5. The correct statement is local: f is 'eventually irreducible mod p^k' roughly when f is irreducible over Q_p, and that is not implied by irreducibility over Q. Factoring mod p^k is still studied algorithmically, but the question as Hilbert posed it is settled (negatively). No source found discusses this diary entry specifically, so the attribution of the answer to Hensel is my inference.
